To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
attachment working models of self versus others govern adults’ preferences and that these preferences are related to depressive symptoms.

(a) the link between attachment and depression was fully mediated by capacity for self-reenforcement and (b ) the link between attachment, depression, and capacity for self-re-enforcement was fully mediated by attachment anxiety and need for reassurances from others.

attachment anxiety is associated with depressive symptoms through a combination of low capacity for self-reassurance and a high need for reassurance of others, whereas attachment avoidance is associated with depressive symptomatology through a low capacity for selfreinforcement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how attachment anxiety, avoidance and depressive symptoms are associated with each other and with two variables: capacity for self-reassurance and need for reassurement from others.
how adults’ working models of attachment influence the development of depressive symptoms.
the role of attachment in depressive symptoms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attachment anxiety, capacity for self-relinforcement, and need of reassurance from others are the most important predictors of depressive symptoms.

attachment working models of self (i.e., attachment avoidance and attachment anxiety) are associated with the capacity for self- and other-reinforcement, respectively, and that the capacity for self and other-reinforcements is associated with depressive symptoms.
the capacity to reinforce oneself and need for reassurement from others mediate the association between depressive symptoms and adult attachment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the attachment working models of self versus others may govern adults' preferences for internal versus external sources of reassurances, which if unavailable, lead them to depression.
attachment anxiety is linked to both internal and external sources of validation, whereas attachment avoidance is linked only to internal sources of validation.

attachment working models of self, others, and the self–other relationship are associated with depressive symptoms, and that the association is partially mediated by capacity for self-revaluation and need for validation from others.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the link between depressive symptomatology and attachment avoidance was fully mediated by capacity for self-reenforcement, whereas the link was partially mediated for attachment anxiety.
attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are differentially linked with depressive symptoms.
attachment working models may govern adults’ reliance on internal vs. external reassurance.
